title: Snake and ladder
scopeHtml:
Scope: requirements, board with a validated jump map, injectable dice, runnable Java and Kotlin, per-game locking, follow-ups.

Scope: requirements, board with a validated jump map, injectable dice, runnable Java and Kotlin, per-game locking, follow-ups.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Design Snake and Ladder for 2 or more players on a 100-square board.

Functional:

  • A board of N squares with snakes (head to lower tail) and ladders (bottom to higher top).
  • Players take turns rolling a die (1 to 6) and move forward by the roll.
  • Landing on a snake head slides down; landing on a ladder bottom climbs up.
  • Exact finish: a roll that would pass the last square is ignored. First to land exactly on the last square wins.

Non-functional: the dice must be injectable (so tests are deterministic), and the board must reject invalid layouts.

Worked example. Player A is on 95 and rolls 6: 101 is over 100, so A stays. Player B is on 92 and rolls 6: lands on 98, which is a snake head to 79, so B drops to 79. A game with no snakes needs about 100 / 3.5 = 29 rolls on average; snakes make it longer.

Industry examples. Game servers (Ludo King, Zynga) keep turn state on the server and use a server-side random generator so clients cannot cheat; the same Game/Board/Dice split is used in chess engines and card games.

Everyday analogy. The physical board game: the board and dice are shared objects, each player is only a token and a name.

Common interview traps.

  • Not asking about the exact-finish rule or extra turn on a 6.
  • Allowing a snake and a ladder to chain forever (a tail that is another head).

notes.title: Core entities
notes.html:
• Dice: interface with roll(). RandomDice for play, a scripted dice for tests.
  • Board: size and a single map from -> to for both snakes and ladders. A snake and a ladder are the same thing (a jump); only the direction differs.
  • Game: players, positions, whose turn, winner. takeTurn() plays one turn.
  • Player: just a String name here. Create a Player class only when it has behaviour (a bot strategy, stats).

Decision gravity. Merging snakes and ladders into one map is a deliberate simplification: fewer classes, and adding "portal" squares needs no new code. The alternative (Snake and Ladder classes) pays off only if they behave differently (a snake with a special animation). Reversible. Validating jumps in the constructor is cheap and prevents infinite-loop bugs.

Everyday analogy. The board is a map with shortcuts and traps drawn on it; the game is the referee.

Common interview traps.

  • Hard-coding Random inside the game; you cannot test it.
  • Applying the jump twice (landing on a ladder top that is also a snake head); forbid chains in validation.

Common interview traps.

  • Drawing Player, Snake and Ladder as full classes with no behaviour.
  • No arrow from Game to Dice: then how do you test?

notes.title: Key patterns
notes.html:
• Dependency injection of Dice (a Strategy). The game does not know where numbers come from; a cheat-proof server dice, a scripted dice, or two dice later.
  • Single responsibility. Board answers "where do I end up?"; Game owns turn order and win; Dice owns randomness.
  • Value-object style board. Immutable after construction, so it can be shared by many games safely (see Concurrency).
  • State (optional). NOT_STARTED, IN_PROGRESS, FINISHED as an enum for the game; not worth classes here.
  • Observer (optional). UI subscribes to "player moved" events.

Industry examples. Java's java.util.Random versus SecureRandom is exactly this Strategy: gaming sites use cryptographic randomness for fairness. Unity and Unreal engines use the same Board/Rules/Dice separation to make game rules testable.

Everyday analogy. A referee (Game) who consults the rulebook (Board) and throws the dice but would happily use any die you hand him.

Common interview traps.

  • Using patterns by name only. Say what change each one absorbs.
  • Making the board mutable so two concurrent games corrupt each other.

notes.title: Code
notes.html:
Java (compiled and run with JDK 21):

import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

interface Dice { int roll(); }

class RandomDice implements Dice {
    private final Random r;
    RandomDice(long seed) { r = new Random(seed); }
    public int roll() { return r.nextInt(6) + 1; }
}

class Board {
    final int size;
    private final Map<Integer, Integer> jumps = new HashMap<>();   // snake head -> tail, ladder bottom -> top

    Board(int size, Map<Integer, Integer> jumps) {
        this.size = size;
        for (var e : jumps.entrySet()) {
            int from = e.getKey(), to = e.getValue();
            if (from <= 1 || from >= size || to < 1 || to > size || from == to)
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad jump " + from + "->" + to);
        }
        for (int to : jumps.values())
            if (jumps.containsKey(to)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("chained jump at " + to); // avoids loops
        this.jumps.putAll(jumps);
    }
    int resolve(int square) { return jumps.getOrDefault(square, square); }
}

class Game {
    protected final Board board;
    protected final Dice dice;
    protected final List<String> players;
    protected final Map<String, Integer> pos = new HashMap<>();
    protected int turn = 0;
    protected String winner;

    Game(Board board, Dice dice, List<String> players) {
        this.board = board; this.dice = dice; this.players = players;
        for (String p : players) pos.put(p, 0);
    }

    /** Plays one turn; returns null when the game is already over. */
    String takeTurn() {
        if (winner != null) return null;
        String p = players.get(turn);
        int roll = dice.roll();
        int target = pos.get(p) + roll;
        if (target <= board.size) {                       // exact finish rule: overshoot = stay
            int landed = board.resolve(target);
            pos.put(p, landed);
            if (landed == board.size) winner = p;
        }
        turn = (turn + 1) % players.size();
        return p + " rolled " + roll + " -> " + pos.get(p);
    }
    boolean over() { return winner != null; }
}

Kotlin core (hand translated, not compiled in this session):

fun interface Dice { fun roll(): Int }

class Board(val size: Int, jumps: Map<Int, Int>) {
    private val jumps = jumps.toMap()
    init {
        jumps.forEach { (from, to) ->
            require(from in 2 until size && to in 1..size && from != to) { "bad jump $from->$to" }
        }
        require(jumps.values.none { it in jumps }) { "chained jump" }
    }
    fun resolve(square: Int) = jumps.getOrDefault(square, square)
}

class Game(private val board: Board, private val dice: Dice, private val players: List<String>) {
    private val pos = players.associateWith { 0 }.toMutableMap()
    private var turn = 0
    var winner: String? = null; private set

    @Synchronized fun takeTurn(): String? {
        if (winner != null) return null
        val p = players[turn]
        val roll = dice.roll()
        val target = pos.getValue(p) + roll
        if (target <= board.size) {
            pos[p] = board.resolve(target)
            if (pos[p] == board.size) winner = p
        }
        turn = (turn + 1) % players.size
        return "$p rolled $roll -> ${pos[p]}"
    }
}

Choices: Map.of boards are immutable. The constructor rejects a jump from square 1 or from the last square, a jump to itself, and chained jumps, because a chain would make resolve need a loop (and a cycle would hang).

Common interview traps.

  • Off by one at the finish: target <= size is allowed, target == size wins.
  • Advancing the turn only when the move is valid; here the turn always advances (an ignored roll still uses the turn).

notes.title: Run and test
notes.html:
public class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Map<Integer, Integer> jumps = Map.of(4, 14, 9, 31, 17, 7, 28, 84, 62, 19, 95, 75, 98, 79);
        Board board = new Board(100, jumps);
        Dice scripted = new Dice() {                      // deterministic dice for the test
            final int[] seq = {3, 1, 6, 6, 2};
            int i = 0;
            public int roll() { return seq[i++ % seq.length]; }
        };
        Game g = new Game(board, scripted, List.of("A", "B"));
        for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) System.out.println(g.takeTurn());
        // A rolled 3 -> 3 ; B rolled 1 -> 1 ; A rolled 6 -> 9 -> ladder 31 ; B rolled 6 -> 7

        SafeGame sg = new SafeGame(board, new RandomDice(42), List.of("A", "B", "C"));
        ExecutorService ex = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);
        List<Future<Integer>> fs = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int t = 0; t < 4; t++)
            fs.add(ex.submit(() -> { int n = 0; while (sg.takeTurn() != null) n++; return n; }));
        int turns = 0; for (Future<Integer> f : fs) turns += f.get();
        ex.shutdown();
        System.out.println("winner = " + sg.winner() + ", turns played in total = " + turns + ", over = " + sg.over());
    }
}

Actual output from javac Demo.java && java Demo:

A rolled 3 -> 3
B rolled 1 -> 1
A rolled 6 -> 31
B rolled 6 -> 7
winner = C, turns played in total = 45, over = true

The scripted dice makes the first four lines predictable: A rolls 3, B rolls 1, A rolls 6 and lands on 9 which is a ladder to 31, B rolls 6 and lands on 7. The last line is the concurrency test; the winner depends on the seed but the shape of the result does not.

Common interview traps.

  • Tests that rely on random games finishing; always use scripted dice for assertions.
  • Not testing the overshoot rule and a snake at 98.

notes.title: Concurrency
notes.html:
Within one game, turns are sequential by definition, but a server receives requests from many threads (each player's phone sends "roll"). If two requests arrive together, both may read the same turn, both roll, and one player plays twice or the winner is set twice.

The fix is a lock around the whole turn: read whose turn, roll, move, set winner, advance. It is a short critical section, so a synchronized method is right. Different games are independent objects, so they run in parallel with no shared lock; the immutable Board is safe to share.

class SafeGame extends Game {
    SafeGame(Board b, Dice d, List<String> players) { super(b, d, players); }
    // roll + move + turn advance is one unit; two threads must never both play the same turn
    @Override synchronized String takeTurn() { return super.takeTurn(); }
    @Override synchronized boolean over() { return super.over(); }
    synchronized String winner() { return winner; }
}

Gravity. One lock per game (not a global lock) keeps scaling linear with the number of games. At a larger scale you route all requests for one game to the same server (consistent hashing on game id) so even the lock stays local; this is how multiplayer back ends shard.

Symptom in production. A player gets two turns in a row, or "winner" flips. The metric: turns played versus number of roll requests accepted.

Everyday analogy. One person holds the dice at a time; others wait until the dice come back to the middle.

Common interview traps.

  • Locking only roll but not the move, so the position is updated from stale data.
  • A global static lock for all games.
  • Letting a player act out of turn because the check was outside the lock.

notes.title: Follow-ups
notes.html:
• Extra turn on a 6. In takeTurn, do not advance when the roll is 6 (cap at 3 sixes in a row).
  • Two dice or a crooked die. Another Dice implementation; no change to Game.
  • Bots and AI players. Introduce a Player interface with Move decide(); with a single die there is nothing to decide, so a bot only matters with choices.
  • Undo and replays. Store each turn as an event (player, roll, from, to) and replay events to rebuild state.
  • Different board sizes and random generated boards. Generate jumps with validation, then check the board is winnable.
  • Persistence. Save positions after each turn so a server restart can resume.

Common interview traps.

  • Overbuilding a Player hierarchy with nothing to differ.
  • Missing that event sourcing gives undo and replay nearly free.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Entities: Dice (interface), Board with one jump map, Game with turn order and winner.
  • Snakes and ladders are the same thing (a jump), validated at construction to forbid chains and bad squares.
  • Dependency-inject the dice for deterministic tests; the board is immutable and shareable.
  • Concurrency: one lock per game covers the whole turn (check turn, roll, move, advance); different games never share a lock.
  • Extensions: extra turns, more dice, bots, event log for undo and replay, persistence.

questions.promptHtml: Why model snakes and ladders as a single from -> to map on the board instead of separate Snake and Ladder classes? What must the board validate?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: They test whether you simplify when two things behave identically and whether you protect invariants in the constructor.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A snake and a ladder do the same thing: if you land on from, you end on to; only the direction differs. One map means fewer classes and portals come free. Separate classes pay off only if they behave differently, for example a snake animation. The board validates in its constructor: no jump from square 1 or the last square, no jump to itself, squares inside the board, and no chain where a jump's target is another jump's start.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
resolve(square) = jumps.getOrDefault(square, square)     // one lookup, no loop

Without the chain rule, resolve would need a loop, and a cycle (a->b, b->a) would hang. Rejecting chains keeps resolve O(1) and loop-free. The board is immutable after construction, so many games can share one board safely.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Separate Player, Snake, Ladder classes with no behaviour.
  • Applying the jump twice (landing on a ladder top that is also a snake head).
  • A mutable board shared by concurrent games.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you tell a snake from a ladder in the UI? -> to < from is a snake; derive it, do not store it.
  2. Why forbid a jump from the last square? -> The game would never finish; the last square is the winning square.
  3. Could you allow chains? -> Yes with a loop and cycle detection, but forbidding is simpler and board designers rarely need it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: draws three classes. Senior: one map, constructor validation with the reasons, and an immutable shared board.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: User-generated boards in a game back end hung a worker when a cycle slipped past validation.

questions.promptHtml: Why is Dice an interface injected into Game, and what does each of Strategy, single responsibility and an immutable board buy you here?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Testability and separation of concerns in a small design; also fairness of randomness.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The game must not know where numbers come from. With a Dice interface I inject a scripted dice in tests (deterministic), a cryptographically strong random on the server so clients cannot cheat, or two dice later. Board answers "where do I end up", Game owns turn order and winner, Dice owns randomness, so each is testable alone. The board is immutable so it can be shared.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Game -> Dice          (who rolls)
Game -> Board -> jumps (where do I land)

java.util.Random versus SecureRandom is exactly this Strategy: the game code does not change. A test uses a scripted dice such as {3, 1, 6, 6, 2}, so the first four turns are predictable.

• new Random() inside Game, so tests cannot control it.
  • Naming patterns without saying what change they absorb.

  2. For real-money style fairness? -> Server-side SecureRandom; log rolls for audit.
  3. Where does Observer fit? -> A UI subscribes to "player moved" events.

questions.contextHtml:
Board size 100. QA reports: a player on 97 who rolls 3 never wins; another on 99 rolls 2 and teleports to square 101 and the game keeps going. The code:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
String takeTurn() {
    String p = players.get(turn);
    int roll = dice.roll();
    int target = pos.get(p) + roll;
    if (target < board.size) {                    // allow move
        pos.put(p, board.resolve(target));
    } else {
        pos.put(p, target);                       // "reached the end"
        winner = p;
    }
    turn = (turn + 1) % players.size();
    return p + " -> " + pos.get(p);
}
fun takeTurn(): String {
    val p = players[turn]
    val roll = dice.roll()
    val target = pos.getValue(p) + roll
    if (target < board.size) pos[p] = board.resolve(target)
    else { pos[p] = target; winner = p }
    turn = (turn + 1) % players.size
    return "$p -> ${pos[p]}"
}
questions.promptHtml: Find the bugs and write the correct rule.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Changes < to <= only and misses that overshoot should be ignored, not winning.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is exact finish required (the notes say yes)? Does an ignored roll consume the turn? Is there an extra turn on 6?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pull the build; the bug affects game results, so fix before more games are played.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Off by one: landing exactly on the last square (target == size) goes to the else branch, which is wrong only if it also resolves jumps; overshoot (target > size) also hits else and wins. Third: the last square never resolves a jump (it should have none).
  4. How I'd verify each: Tests: 97 + 3 = 100 wins; 99 + 2 stays on 99 and the game continues; 98 snake case.
  5. Root cause: Win and overshoot are one branch.
  6. Fix: if (target <= size) { landed = resolve(target); pos = landed; if (landed == size) winner = p; }. Overshoot leaves the position unchanged, and the turn still advances.
  7. Prevention: Boundary tests: size-1, size, size+1, snake at 98.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not special-case the last square inside resolve; the validation already forbids a jump from it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Allow overshoot to bounce back from the end? -> Another rule; implement as a FinishRule strategy, not a flag.
  • Should an ignored roll keep the turn? -> Product decision; the notes' rule: the turn advances.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A win condition coded as >= size rather than == size gave players the win from overshooting; the leaderboard was wrong for weeks.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: flips < to <= only.
  • Hire: separates overshoot, wins only on landing exactly, with tests.
  • Strong hire: boundary table of tests and a rule-as-strategy mention.

questions.contextHtml: Product wants: a roll of 6 gives an extra turn, three sixes in a row forfeit the third move and the turn passes, a second game mode uses two dice, and a fixed-sequence "crooked" dice for the tutorial.
questions.promptHtml: Which classes change, and show the code change for the extra-turn rule.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Edits Game with if (mode == ...) branches for every mode.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does an extra turn after a ladder count? Does the six count if the move was ignored by the overshoot rule? Do sixes reset per player?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None; plan the change and add tests first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Two dice and a crooked dice are new Dice implementations; the extra turn is a change inside takeTurn only.
  4. How I'd verify each: Scripted dice {6, 6, 6} and {6, 3} to cover forfeit and extra turn.
  5. Root cause (design): planned extension.
  6. Fix: Dice implementations: TwoDice, ScriptedDice; no change to Game.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
int roll = dice.roll();
sixes = (roll == 6) ? sixes + 1 : 0;
if (sixes == 3) { sixes = 0; turn = (turn + 1) % players.size(); return p + " three sixes, turn lost"; }
move(p, roll);
if (roll != 6) turn = (turn + 1) % players.size();      // a six keeps the turn
val roll = dice.roll()
sixes = if (roll == 6) sixes + 1 else 0
if (sixes == 3) { sixes = 0; turn = (turn + 1) % players.size; return "$p three sixes, turn lost" }
move(p, roll)
if (roll != 6) turn = (turn + 1) % players.size         // a six keeps the turn

sixes is a per-game counter, reset whenever the turn passes. 7. Prevention: The scripted-dice tests above stay in CI. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: With many rules (extra turns, bonus, penalty) I would extract a TurnRule strategy. I would not add a Player hierarchy: a single die gives a bot nothing to decide.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• With two dice, what counts as six? -> A rule on the sum or on doubles; put it in a TurnRule, not in Dice.
  • Who tracks sixes under concurrency? -> The game, inside the same per-game lock.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An extra-turn rule implemented outside the lock gave some players three moves in a row.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: mode flags in Game.
  • Hire: new Dice classes and a small change inside takeTurn, tested with scripted dice.
  • Strong hire: TurnRule strategy, per-game state under lock.

questions.contextHtml:
A level editor lets designers upload boards. You review the constructor, which only checks from < size and to >= 1. Three uploaded boards:

Board A: 98->79, 79->40, 40->12        (chain of snakes)
Board B: 99->10 and 10->99             (cycle)
Board C: 94->50, 95->51, 96->52, 97->53, 98->54, 99->55   (every square past 93 is a snake)

Board B hung a worker in production; Board C was "valid" but playtesters could not finish.
questions.promptHtml: What validations do you add and which problems cannot be caught by simple local checks?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds a cycle check and calls it done.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is chaining a desired feature? Are boards user generated or reviewed? What is the max size?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reject chains and cycles in the constructor so resolve is a single lookup; fix the stuck workers with a timeout.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Chains (A) need either a loop or rejection; the cycle (B) hangs a loop; C is a reachability problem: no valid path to the last square.
  4. How I'd verify each: Local checks: from in 2..size-1, to in 1..size, from != to, no jump target is also a start (kills A and B). For C: a BFS over squares where each roll 1..6 moves forward and resolves jumps; the board is winnable if the last square is reachable from 0.
  5. Root cause: Validation only covered local properties.
  6. Fix: Add the BFS reachability check on the board's construction (cost O(size x 6), tiny).
  7. Prevention: Property test: generated random boards are either rejected or winnable; keep the validation in the constructor so no unvalidated board can exist.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: BFS tells winnability, not fairness (expected game length); a fairness check is a separate tool. I would not throw generic exceptions; a validation result with a message helps the editor UI.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not allow chains and resolve in a loop? -> Then cycles need detection; the rule "no chains" is O(1) and simple.
  • Is a board with six consecutive snakes (a "wall") winnable? -> Only if the roll set of 1..6 can jump over the wall; six consecutive heads can block progress entirely, the BFS catches this.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A community board with a snake cycle looped a game worker at 100 percent CPU until the pod was killed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cycle check only.
  • Hire: local checks plus BFS reachability.
  • Strong hire: explains why local checks cannot catch the wall, adds property tests and UI-friendly validation errors.

questions.contextHtml:
On a server handling roll requests from phones, support reports "player B played twice in a row" and "two winners announced". Log excerpt for game g-77:

12:00:01.120 g-77 req r1 player=A roll=4 pos 17->21
12:00:01.121 g-77 req r2 player=A roll=6 pos 17->23     <- same player, same position read
12:00:01.121 g-77 winner=A  (announced)
12:00:01.124 g-77 winner=B  (announced)

Each phone sends "roll" and retries on timeout after 2 s. takeTurn has no lock. The Board is immutable.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the race, the retry problem and your fix. How does the design scale to many games?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make takeTurn synchronized" and nothing about retries or other servers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Single server or several? Is the request carrying the player id from a token? Does the client send a request id on retry?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a per-game lock around the whole turn.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Two threads read the same turn and the same position, both roll, both write (lost update). Second: a client retry makes the same roll request twice. Third: the check "is it your turn" ran outside the lock.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log request ids; test with 4 threads calling takeTurn and assert every accepted turn alternates players.
  5. Root cause: Check-then-act on turn state with no mutual exclusion; no idempotency on retries.
  6. Fix: synchronized (or a ReentrantLock) per game around the whole sequence: check whose turn, roll, move, set winner, advance. Validate that the requester is the current player inside the lock. Add an idempotency key per request so a retry returns the earlier result and does not roll again.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
synchronized String takeTurn(String requester, String reqId) {
    if (winner != null) return null;
    if (!requester.equals(players.get(turn))) throw new IllegalStateException("not your turn");
    String done = results.get(reqId);
    if (done != null) return done;                // retry: same answer, no second roll
    String out = super.takeTurn();
    results.put(reqId, out);
    return out;
}
@Synchronized fun takeTurn(requester: String, reqId: String): String? {
    if (winner != null) return null
    check(requester == players[turn]) { "not your turn" }
    results[reqId]?.let { return it }             // retry: same answer, no second roll
    return playTurn().also { results[reqId] = it }
}
  1. Prevention: Metric: roll requests accepted versus turns recorded; a multi-thread test per release.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The lock is per game, never global, so different games run in parallel. The idempotency map must be bounded (per game, cleared at game end). I would not lock only roll or only the move.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not make the fields volatile? -> Visibility without atomicity; check-then-act is still racy.
  • Is the immutable Board an issue? -> No, shared reads are safe.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "double move" report in a game turned out to be a mobile retry on a flaky network, not a lock problem; the idempotency key fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: synchronizes roll only.
  • Hire: per-game lock around the full turn, validates the player inside the lock.
  • Strong hire: idempotency keys and the accepted-versus-recorded metric.

questions.contextHtml: A single server holds all active games in a ConcurrentHashMap. The product expects 2 million concurrent games at peak, a roll every 15 s per game on average, and 30 percent of games idle. Each game state is about 200 bytes. A turn must complete under 100 ms p99, and a server restart must not lose games.
questions.promptHtml: Do the capacity math, design the sharding, and say where the lock lives.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Scale horizontally with Redis" without numbers or ordering guarantees.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the roll rate average or peak? Must turn order be strictly consistent (yes)? Can a game's moves be served by any node? What persistence guarantee after a crash?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None; this is capacity design.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Rolls per second: 2M / 15 s is about 133,000 per second; memory 2M x 200 B = 400 MB, which fits on one machine, so the problem is CPU and availability, not memory. A turn is microseconds of work, so the lock cost is negligible; the dominating costs are network and persistence.
  4. How I'd verify each: Load test one node with recorded traffic; measure per-turn CPU and p99.
  5. Root cause (design): a single node is a single point of failure and a throughput ceiling.
  6. Fix: Shard by game id (consistent hashing) so all requests for one game reach one owner node, where an in-process per-game lock suffices. Persist each turn as an append-only event (game id, sequence number, player, roll, from, to) so a restart replays state. If a game must be served from anywhere, store it in Redis or a DB and use optimistic concurrency: version number and compare-and-set; the loser retries or is rejected.
  7. Prevention: Metrics for turns per second, rejected stale-version writes, p99 per node, reconciliation of event log versus game state.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Sticky routing gives simple locking but needs failover (a node dies, the shard map reassigns and a new node loads games from the log). Optimistic writes avoid affinity but add a round trip per turn. I would not use a global distributed lock.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• One node dies mid-turn? -> The new owner replays events; a turn without a persisted event is treated as not happened and the client retries with its idempotency key.
  • Rebalancing hot shards? -> Move whole games, never split one game across nodes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A game service sharded by user id instead of game id; two players in one game landed on different nodes and every move needed a distributed lock.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "use Redis" with no numbers.
  • Hire: 133k/s and 400 MB math, shard by game id, event log.
  • Strong hire: failover story, idempotency, optimistic versioning alternative, honest trade-offs.

questions.contextHtml: The PM says: "add undo, spectators who can replay games, and let the game survive a server restart." Nothing more. A colleague proposes saving the full position map to a database after each turn and adding an undo() that restores the previous snapshot.
questions.promptHtml: What questions do you ask first, and what is your design?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Snapshots only, with no thought about who may undo or the dice.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who may undo (the last mover, any player, vote)? How many levels? Does undo reroll the dice or restore the roll? Are spectators live or delayed? Must replays be bit-exact? Rules versions (a replay under new rules)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None; scope first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Undo in a dice game is odd (it changes randomness) so product must define it; an event log (player, roll, from, to) gives replay, undo (pop the last event and recompute or apply the inverse) and persistence together.
  4. How I'd verify each: A property test: replaying the event list from an empty game yields the same final positions as the live game.
  5. Root cause (design): State snapshots lose history; events keep it.
  6. Fix: Event log as the source of truth: each turn appends an event with a sequence number. Current state is a fold of events (cache it). Persistence: append events to a store, rebuild on restart. Spectators subscribe to the event stream or poll by sequence. Undo: append an Undone(seq) event (never delete history) and recompute.
  7. Prevention: Version the event schema and the board id so old games replay under the same rules; a replay test in CI.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Events cost storage (small here, about tens of bytes per turn) and need folding; snapshots every N events cap rebuild time. I would not overbuild a Player hierarchy or CQRS machinery for this size.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The rules change after release? -> Store the board and rules version on the game; replay with that version.
  • Red herring: "use a database transaction for undo". -> Undo is a domain event, not a DB rollback.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A game kept only the latest positions; when a cheating dispute arrived, there was no history to prove who rolled what.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: snapshot per turn, no questions.
  • Hire: event log gives replay, undo and recovery.
  • Strong hire: asks the product questions first, handles versioning and snapshots, and keeps history append-only.
